where $\conv$ denotes the convex hull of a set.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof only computes a gradient, which requires singleton extreme eigenvalues (Lemma lem:optkappacond). The 'if and only if' criterion x1•x1 = xn•xn is therefore proved only in the smooth case, and the singleton hypothesis is not even stated. For repeated λmax or λmin, optimality means that 0 lies in the (convex-hull) subdifferential. This amounts to diag(X1W1X1^T) = diag(XnWnXn^T) for some PSD trace-one weight matrices W1, Wn. The statement instead asserts that one can pick single eigenvectors with x1•x1 = xn•xn, i.e. rank-one W's. That condition is in general stronger, and no argument is given for it.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the singleton hypothesis for the gradient criterion. For the nonsmooth case, replace the claim with the convex-hull condition: there exist PSD trace-one W1, Wn with diag(X1W1X1^T) = diag(XnWnXn^T). Prove it via 0 ∈ ∂(λmax − κλmin) at d = e.
issues.overall_effect: The optimality characterization is unsupported (and generally too strong as a necessary condition) whenever the extreme eigenvalues are multiple. The smooth singleton case, used in prop:nonuniqd and lem:optAforkappaconstr, survives.
issues.title: Nonsmooth κ-optimality characterization uses single eigenvector pairs instead of the convex-hull subdifferential condition
issues.why_classification: A contained new argument (a subdifferential computation for the convex function λmax − κλmin) is needed and the nonsmooth statement changes form. The smooth result and the algorithms are unaffected.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Second, since \Cref{GD} is a subgradient method, in general it is not a descent method.

issues.failure_explanation: The cited Kiwiel result gives only liminf κ(d_k) = κ*, which implies that the record values κ*^k decrease to κ*. It does not imply that κ(d_k) itself is monotone. The paper explicitly says the method is not a descent method, so the 'in particular' conclusion about κ(d_k) is unsupported and generally false.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the conclusion with κ*^k ↓ κ*, using the record values the theorem already defines.
issues.overall_effect: The stated monotone-convergence guarantee for the iterates is not established; only liminf and record-value convergence hold.
issues.title: Asymptotic theorem claims monotone decrease of iterate objective values
issues.why_classification: A one-line restatement using the already defined record values gives the correct conclusion with no loss of the asymptotic guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $AD=A\blkdiag(R_i)\blkdiag(R_i^T)$ are equal to the eigenvalues of

issues.failure_explanation: The ω-value of B^T A B depends only on B B^T, and optimality requires B_i B_i^T ∝ A_i^{-1} = (R_i^T R_i)^{-1}. The choice B_i = R_i^{-T} gives (R_i R_i^T)^{-1} instead, which differs in general. Example: A = [1 1; 1 2], R = [1 1; 0 1], k = 1. Then B^T A B has trace 3 and determinant 1, so ω = 1.5 rather than the optimal value 1. The displayed eigenvalue identity also uses R_i rather than R_i^{-1}, giving D = blkdiag(R_i R_i^T), which is unrelated to A_i^{-1}.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Take B_i = R_i^{-1}, so that B_i B_i^T = A_i^{-1}. Then state that the eigenvalues of A·blkdiag(R_i^{-1}R_i^{-T}) equal those of blkdiag(R_i^{-T}) A blkdiag(R_i^{-1}).
issues.overall_effect: The claimed recovery of the partial Cholesky preconditioner as an ω-optimal block diagonal preconditioner is not justified as written.
issues.title: Partial-Cholesky corollary uses wrong Cholesky factor (R_i^{-T}) and non-inverted factors
issues.why_classification: A short local correction, consistent with cor:blckdiag, restores the claim with no new argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \Cref{Subgrad V} was $145.0$ times faster than \cite{doi:10.1287/opre.2022.0592} while \Cref{alg:GDeplustVv}
our proposed methods consistently achieved much greater reductions in $\kappa$

issues.failure_explanation: The conclusion claims both methods were over 200 times faster on SuiteSparse. The paper's own averages are 145.0× for Algorithm 2.2 and 397.8× for Algorithm C.1, and per-instance ratios go as low as 1.3–2.0×. It also claims 'consistently' greater κ reductions, yet the baseline beats Algorithm 2.2 on several instances (99% vs 90%, 94% vs 74%, 92% vs 83%) and beats Algorithm C.1 on some as well.

failure_location.quote: our two subgradient methods significantly outperformed (over $200$ times faster) the SDP-based approach

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the speedups as the reported averages (145× and 398×) and describe the κ reductions as larger on average rather than consistently.
issues.overall_effect: The summary of computational advantages is materially exaggerated relative to the reported data.
issues.title: Conclusion overstates speedups and consistency of κ reductions relative to the tables
issues.why_classification: Correcting the prose to match the paper's own tables preserves all formal results and the empirical conclusions.
